qs.q: Mutation of the RB1 gene promotes cancer development by affecting cell cycle regulation at which specific transition?
o: G0 to G1 cell cycle transition
G1 to S cell cycle transition
G2 to M cell cycle transition
qs.e: RB normally holds the cell at the G1/S checkpoint until it is ready to divide, and losing it removes this vital brake. It does not primarily regulate the G2/M or metaphase checkpoints.
qs.s: Pathology by Dr. Irungu — Study Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Mutation or loss of the RB1 gene promotes cancer development by producing which of the following cell cycle effects?
o: Removing a checkpoint that blocks the G1/S transition
Preventing DNA replication during the S phase
qs.e: RB normally holds the cell cycle at the G1/S checkpoint until it is ready to divide. Losing this protein removes the crucial brake, allowing uncontrolled cell cycle progression.
qs.s: Pathology by Dr. Irungu — Study Notes — Oncopathology: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with a soft tissue mass. Histopathological examination reveals an inactivating mutation of the retinoblastoma (RB) protein. Which direct consequence is expected in the cell cycle of these tumour cells?
o: Unrestrained progression from G1 to S phase due to constant E2F release
Permanent arrest in the G0 quiescent state by hypophosphorylated RB
Activation of the spindle assembly checkpoint to block anaphase entry
Inhibition of cyclin-dependent kinases by accumulated p16 proteins
qs.e: When RB is lost or mutated, it can no longer bind and inactivate E2F transcription factors, leading to uncontrolled proliferation through unchecked G1/S transition. Hypophosphorylated normal RB blocks the cell cycle, but mutant RB fails to exert this brake.
qs.s: Molecular Basis of Cancer: Cell Cycle, Apoptosis & Angiogenesis — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: During which phase of the cell cycle does normal DNA replication occur, and which class of chemotherapy drugs primarily targets this phase?
qs.e: DNA replication occurs during the S phase, making it the most sensitive phase for antimetabolites. In contrast, alkylating agents are cell cycle non-specific.
qs.s: Cancer Pharmacology: Cell Cycle, Oncogenes & Drug Targets — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: A patient presents with a malignancy linked to a mutation in a tumor suppressor gene responsible for blocking the G1/S cell cycle transition. Which gene is most likely mutated?
qs.e: RB1 is a key tumor suppressor gene that normally blocks the G1/S cell cycle transition. Conversely, HER2, RAS, and MYC are proto-oncogenes.
qs.s: Cancer Pharmacology: Cell Cycle, Oncogenes & Drug Targets — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: What is the fundamental mechanism by which taxanes (such as paclitaxel and docetaxel) arrest cells in the M phase of the cell cycle?
qs.e: Taxanes stabilize microtubules and prevent their depolymerization, trapping the cell in mitosis. Inhibiting tubulin polymerization is the distinct mechanism of vinca alkaloids.
qs.s: Cancer Pharmacology: Cell Cycle, Oncogenes & Drug Targets — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which specific cyclin-CDK complex is responsible for the initial phosphorylation of the retinoblastoma (RB) protein during the mid-G1 phase of the normal cell cycle?
o: Activation of the Cyclin E-CDK2 complex
Activation of the Cyclin D-CDK4 complex
Activation of the Cyclin A-CDK2 complex
Activation of the Cyclin B-CDK1 complex
qs.e: Cyclin D rises first in mid-G1 and binds CDK4 to form the Cyclin D-CDK4 complex, which phosphorylates RB protein to drive cell cycle progression. Cyclin E-CDK2 acts later at the G1/S restriction point.
qs.s: Hallmarks of Cancer: Molecular Basis, Cell Cycle & Oncogenes — Notes: MCQs

qs.q: Which gene type is known as the guardian of the genome and controls the crucial G1/S cell cycle checkpoint?
qs.e: The p53 gene is a critical tumor suppressor that controls the G1/S checkpoint to prevent abnormal cell proliferation. DNA repair genes fix errors rather than directly serving as cell cycle checkpoints.
qs.s: Oncology Intro: Cancer Biology, Genetics & Immuno-Oncology — Notes: MCQs

es.q: Name two distinct chemotherapeutic agents that primarily exert their cytotoxic effects during the S phase of the cell cycle, and briefly describe the critical cellular process that occurs during this phase.
es.m: Two drugs targeting the S phase are Methotrexate and 5-Fluorouracil (or Cytarabine, Gemcitabine). The critical cellular process occurring in the S phase is DNA synthesis or replication, where the cell copies its genetic material in preparation for division.
es.s: Cell Cycle & Chemotherapy: Drug Mechanisms & Phases — Practice Questions — Essay

es.q: Outline three distinct characteristics of Cell Cycle Specific (CCS) chemotherapeutic agents that influence their clinical administration and effectiveness.
es.m: Three characteristics of Cell Cycle Specific (CCS) chemotherapeutic agents are: 1. They only kill cells actively going through a specific phase of the cell cycle. 2. They are useless against cells in the G0 (resting) phase. 3. They require prolonged exposure (e.g., continuous infusions or frequent doses) to be effective. 4. They are generally more effective against fast-growing tumors.
es.s: Cell Cycle & Chemotherapy: Drug Mechanisms & Phases — Practice Questions — Essay

es.q: A medical oncologist is considering chemotherapy for a patient with a bulky, slow-growing solid tumor. Explain why a Non-Cell Cycle Specific (NCCS) chemotherapeutic agent would generally be preferred over a Cell Cycle Specific (CCS) agent for this type of malignancy, providing two reasons based on t
es.m: NCCS agents are preferred for bulky, slow-growing tumors for two main reasons: 1. NCCS drugs kill cells at any phase of the cell cycle, including G0 (resting phase). Slow-growing or bulky tumors often have a significant proportion of cells in G0, which would be resistant to CCS agents. 2. They can be effective with a single large dose and do not require the prolonged exposure necessary for CCS drugs, making them more suitable for targeting a mixed population of dividing and resting cells in less proliferative tumors.
es.s: Cell Cycle & Chemotherapy: Drug Mechanisms & Phases — Practice Questions — Essay

es.q: Describe the G0 phase of the cell cycle in the context of chemotherapy. Name one class of chemotherapeutic agents that remains effective against cells in this particular phase.
es.m: The G0 phase is a resting state where cells are not actively dividing or preparing for division. In the context of chemotherapy, many cancer cells, particularly in slow-growing tumors, can reside in G0, rendering them insensitive to Cell Cycle Specific (CCS) agents. The class of chemotherapeutic agents that remains effective against cells in the G0 phase is Alkylating agents.
es.s: Cell Cycle & Chemotherapy: Drug Mechanisms & Phases — Practice Questions — Essay

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: The cell cycle is a tightly regulated series of events leading to cell division. Dysregulation, often due to DNA damage or mutations in key proteins like p53 and RB, can lead to uncontrolled proliferation and cancer.

sections.p: The cell cycle is the ordered sequence of events a cell undergoes to grow and divide. It comprises distinct phases: G1 (growth), S (DNA synthesis), G2 (preparation for mitosis), and M (mitosis). Normal cell cycle progression is crucial for tissue repair and development. Diagnosis of cell cycle abnormalities is usually made by identifying the consequences, such as tumour formation.
b: Key regulators: p53 ('guardian of the genome'), RB gene.
Loss of control leads to uncontrolled proliferation.

sections.p: Genetic mutations are the primary cause of cell cycle dysregulation. These can affect genes encoding cell cycle regulators like p53 and RB. Viral infections, such as HPV (via E6 protein degrading p53), can also disrupt cell cycle control. Environmental factors like radiation and chemical carcinogens can induce DNA damage, leading to mutations.
b: Mutations in tumour suppressor genes (e.g., p53, RB).

sections.p: The most common clinical presentation of cell cycle dysregulation is cancer. Tumours arise from uncontrolled cell division and can manifest with a wide range of symptoms depending on their location, size, and whether they have metastasized. Cells in G0/G1 are often found in tumours.
b: Symptoms vary by tumour type and location.
Cells in G0/G1 are common in tumours.

t.b: To identify abnormal cell morphology and proliferation patterns indicative of malignancy. Microscopic examination of tissue biopsy is the gold standard for cancer diagnosis.
To detect specific proteins (e.g., Ki-67 for proliferation index, p53 overexpression) that indicate cell cycle activity and prognosis. Useful when standard histology is equivocal.
To analyse DNA content and cell cycle phase distribution in a cell population. Helps in classifying leukaemias and lymphomas and assessing ploidy.

sections.p: The main red flag is the presence of a palpable mass or unexplained bleeding. Complications include tumour invasion into vital organs, metastasis to distant sites, and paraneoplastic syndromes. Uncontrolled proliferation can lead to organ failure and death.

Management focuses on eradicating or controlling the abnormal cell proliferation. This typically involves surgery to remove the tumour, chemotherapy to kill rapidly dividing cells, radiation therapy to damage DNA and induce apoptosis, and targeted therapies that interfere with specific cell cycle pathways.
b: Chemotherapy to target rapidly dividing cells.
Radiation therapy to induce DNA damage.
Targeted therapies against cell cycle proteins.

sections.p: Follow-up involves regular monitoring for recurrence or metastasis through clinical examination and imaging. Prevention strategies include avoiding carcinogens, vaccination against oncogenic viruses (e.g., HPV), and promoting healthy lifestyles. Early detection through screening is key.

Benign neoplasms can be confused with malignant tumours due to similar growth patterns. Inflammatory processes can sometimes mimic tumour growth. Conditions causing hyperplasia (increase in cell number) may also be mistaken for neoplastic proliferation.

A normal proliferation index (e.g., Ki-67) does not rule out malignancy, as some slow-growing cancers have low proliferation rates. Conversely, high proliferation rates can be seen in benign conditions like reactive hyperplasia. Tumour markers can be elevated in non-malignant conditions.
b: Normal proliferation index in some cancers.
Tumour markers elevated in non-malignant states.

faq.q: What are the main phases of the cell cycle?
faq.a: The main phases are G1 (growth), S (DNA synthesis), G2 (preparation for mitosis), and M (mitosis).

faq.q: What is the role of p53 in the cell cycle?
faq.a: p53, the 'guardian of the genome', triggers cell cycle arrest or apoptosis if DNA damage is irreparable.

faq.q: How does HPV affect the cell cycle?
faq.a: HPV's E6 protein degrades p53, leading to loss of cell cycle control and promoting cancer development.

exam: Describe the phases of the cell cycle and the role of key regulatory proteins like p53 and RB.
Explain how disruptions in cell cycle control can lead to the development of cancer.
